message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, the evidence doesn't support that, and the line you found points the other way, if anything. The two control offices cut meetings without reducing hours and saw a 4.1% per-hour rise. That suggests part of the gain may be available *without* the hours cut. But it's only two offices with no comparison group, so it doesn't establish that either. The report says explicitly that the question is open, and no study in this evidence base had an arm that reorganised work without cutting hours.

The report also offers the other possibility: the hours cut may be what *prompts* the reorganisation and makes it stick. That's plausible, but it hasn't been tested.

Suggested wording for the paper:

> It is not yet known whether the hours reduction itself is necessary for the gain. In the Varden trial, about half the per-hour improvement was associated with fewer recurring meetings, and two comparison offices that cut meetings without reducing hours also saw a smaller gain (4.1%), though this was unplanned and uncontrolled. Whether reorganising work alone would capture much of the benefit, or whether the shorter week is what drives that reorganisation, has not been tested.

If the board wants an answer, the obvious next step is a trial with a third arm in which offices cut meetings but keep their current hours. That arm would also be cheaper to run than the shorter week itself.
